> **Weakness 3.**  While the score is motivated by minimizing $P(|C(X)|>1) + \lambda E(|C(X)|)$, similar composite losses can potentially be handled within existing efficiency-oriented frameworks (e.g., [5]) . Please clarify why a new score is necessary rather than adapting losses within those frameworks, and whether SOCOP can be integrated into them while preserving nestedness, monotonicity, and computational benefits.

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. The efficiency-oriented frameworks in [5, 6] has a core difference from ours. As the reviewer suggested, if we use our composite loss $P(|C(X)|>1) + \lambda E(|C(X)|)$ in the efficiency-oriented framework, it actually uses this loss as a metric to select a score from pre-specified candidates $\Lambda = \\{S^1, S^2, \dots\\}$. This is fundamentally different from directly optimizing a loss to derive a score (our work). **Thus, we do not think that the two approaches aim to solve the same problem, making them not directly comparable in our setting.** For example, take $\Lambda=\\{S^{LAS}, S^{APS}, S^{RAPS}\\}$, (here we assume we have enough data to split into tuning/calibration/test sets to avoid selection bias, like we did in our experiments).  The best score on the tuning set will determine the performance on the test set, and will be exactly that of the corresponding baseline/score reported in our tables. 

In other words, the loss is only a selection metric among several candidate scores, and does not fundamentally improve them. 
In contrast, in our case, the loss determines the construction of the score, which can potentially lead to an improved performance compared to a fixed set of baseline scores. In addition, integrating our loss into [5] would require first tuning $\lambda$ beofre proceeding to select the score. This would introduce the additional difficulty of selecting the hyperparameter $\lambda$, and their framework would have to be potentially extended to allow the selection of not just non-conformity scores but also loss functions. (At the outset, at least, their loss function is fixed and pre-specified.) 

For the second question, in principle, our SOCOP can be integrated into those frameworks while preserving nestedness, monotonicity, and computational benefits, as these properties are only related to the score computation. However, our score also depends on $\lambda$. One possible way to deal with this challenge is to fix the same $\lambda$ for both the score and the loss, i.e., $\Lambda=\\{S^{SOCOP}_\lambda, \text{other scores}\\}$ with the selection loss $\mathcal{L}=P(|C(X)|>1) + \lambda E(|C(X)|)$, but this again goes back to the above hyperparameter selection problem. In contrast, our work provides a flexible way to choose the $\lambda$ based on the tradeoff (Figure 2, Sec. 3.1.1) between size and multiple labels rate. Practitioners can choose the $\lambda$ based on their own preference.

We will add this discussion to our paper. 

> **Question 1.** The definition of a singleton set should be more precise. The definition used in the formulas is $|C(X)|\leq 1$
, which differs from $|C(X)|= 1$. Empty prediction sets can occur in conformal prediction. For example, if $\hat{p}$ can almost perfectly predict the true class, then approximately an $\alpha$ fraction of least ambiguous sets will be empty. If we use $|C(X)|= 1$ as the definition of a singleton set and change the first term of the loss in line 135 to $I(|C(X)|\neq 1)$, this may harm the monotonicity of the score function.

We thank the reviewer for this key observation. We agree that a singleton set should precisely refer to $|C(X)|=1$. 
Our use of the "singleton objective" was imprecise. This objective is formally known as the M-criterion (for multiple labels) from [7]. Since we found the term M-criterion a bit too terse and non-descriptive, we decided to choose the more descriptive term "singleton objective"; However, we agree that its meaning needs to be more precise. We will add a clarification about the precise meaning of singletons, but if the reviewer agrees with us, we would like to keep the current terminology. Please let us know, and we are happy to discuss further.

Across all datasets used in our paper, we observe that empty prediction sets occur in fewer than 0.01\% of test instances for all methods, except for RAPS (roughly 0.1\%). Hence, we do not report this metric in the text as its effect is completely negligible. However, in the revision, we will add a footnote about this issue.

model selection. arXiv preprint arXiv:2408.07066, 2024.

summary.value: The paper proposes a new nonconformity score with the goal of reducing the probability of producing non-singleton sets. The score is motivated by an optimization problem that optimizes a combination of the singleton objective and the expected length of the prediction sets subject to coverage constraint. The authors provide an efficient algorithm through a geometric reformulation to compute the nonconformity score. The paper includes empirical evaluation on image classification and LLM multiple-choice question answering that shows the proposed method reduces average set size and increases the frequency of singleton predictions.

strengths.value: The motivation behind the problem of singleton sets is important in practical settings. The paper presents a theoretically sound and efficient algorithm for the problem. Empirical evaluation shows that the method reduces the non-singleton probability while maintaining the average set size. Additionally, the extensions discussed in Section 2.2 are appreciated.

weaknesses.value:
1. The paper is not written very clearly and it is hard to follow. The notation is extensive and dense in Section 2, with several new symbols introduced with little intuition. Additionally, the definition of nested conformal prediction was deferred for later, while the concepts are used in the paper; e.g., l215 ‘the nested sets property implies that…’ – this hampers the readability of the paper. It is suggested to work on this in the revised version.
2. While the paper guarantees marginal validity, there is no discussion on the implications of this objective on conditional coverage. Such analysis (theoretical and empirical) is warranted to understand the underlying tradeoffs.
3. Apart from Coverage and Avg Size, the empirical evaluation should report metrics that measure adaptivity of the sets e.g., worst-slice coverage, SSCV. The current evaluation is limited in its scope of studying the Avg Size and P(Size > 1) that are directly optimized by the method. To understand the usefulness of the sets, the analysis will benefit from additional metrics.

**RAPS outperforms APS in both Average size and SSCV**, which is consistent with the findings in RAPS paper. As we replied to Reviewer XEKF, we did not include APS as a separate baseline because we consider RAPS as a stronger version of APS.


2. 
To change $|C(X)|>1$ to $|C(X)|\neq 1$, we would need to go from the very beginning,  rephrasing and replacing  all mathematical results and experiments in our paper completely. 
As we mentioned in our first reply, we used $|C(X)|>1$ as it originates from the M-criterion in [7]. Since we found the term M-criterion a bit too terse and non-descriptive, we decided to choose the more descriptive term "singleton objective”, though it's not completely precise. We have added a footnote at line 051 to clarify this in the revised version.

In addition, thanks to Reviewer 67Nw's question, we also analyzed the probability of empty sets from a theoretical perspective. When $\lambda=0$ (pure singleton limit, see Section 2.2, Corollary 2.5), the resulting split conformal prediction sets are either the top-1 label $\left\\{y_1\right\\}$ if $\hat{p}\left(y_1 \mid x_{n+1}\right) \geqslant c$, for some quantity $c$, or the whole set $\mathcal{Y}$ otherwise. Hence, the procedure will never produce empty sets. However, we agree that when $\lambda>0$, the method can produce empty sets. In our construction, the prediction set at a test point $x$ is $\widehat{C}(x)=\left\\{y: r_\lambda(x, y) \leq \hat{q}\right\\}$, where $\hat{q}$ is the calibrated threshold. Because the scores are non-decreasing, i.e., $r_\lambda(x, y_1)\leq r_\lambda(x, y_2)\leq...\leq r_\lambda(x, y_K)$, $\widehat{C}(x)=\varnothing$ is equivalent to $r_\lambda(x, y_1)>\hat{q}$. One can show that $r_\lambda\left(x, y_1\right)=\frac{\lambda}{\hat{p}\left(y_1 \mid x\right)}$, hence $\widehat{C}(x)=\varnothing$ if and only if $\hat{p}\left(y_1 \mid x\right)<\frac{\lambda}{\hat{q}}$. A typical situation in which this happens is when the model is very uncertain about an input x, the probability of its top prediction, $\hat{p}(y_1|x)$, can be lower than $\frac{\lambda}{\hat{q}}$, resulting in an empty set. In such cases, SOCOP produces an empty set, which can be viewed as the model appropriately abstaining from prediction due to low confidence.

Most importantly, **empirically, the rate of empty sets for SOCOP was negligible** (<0.01%) across all experiments, which was comparable to other baseline methods. Thus, in our setting, using $I(|C(X)|>1)$ rather than $I(|C(X)| \neq 1)$ does not affect the conclusions or the practical utility of the method.
 Therefore, we do not see a utilitarian justification for going through the effort of changing everything (which may take several weeks of work) because the outcomes do not change in any significant way in the experiments reported in our paper. In short, we do not believe it is reasonable to expect such extensive modifications and a complete rerun of all experiments---especially in a short rebuttal period---given that they do not lead to any valuable outcome for the community.

 We hope that our arguments sound reasonable to the reviewer. However, if there is absolutely no way that the reviewer agrees, then we would rather change the name of our method to "Multiplicity Optimized Conformal Prediction" (MOCOP) to ensure consistency of the terminology and objective.

summary.value: The paper targets increasing the probability that conformal prediction sets are singletons (sets of size one) in multi-class classification. It proposes a new nonconformity score derived from a Lagrangian relaxation of a joint objective balancing singleton frequency and expected set size, and introduces an O(K) per-instance algorithm via a lower convex hull construction. Empirically, the method increases singleton frequency with small impact on average set size while maintaining marginal coverage.

I thank the authors for their detailed response. 

A couple of comments and suggestions:

- Thanks for sharing the SSCV results. While I do not expect the authors to report new results with WSC, I would like to point that PCA with the logits layer for ImageNet is feasible and prior works have adopted a similar method.

**We implemented and tested the aggregated score $S_\{\lambda,\eta\}^\{\mathrm{AGG}\}$
proposed by the reviewer.** This score requires hyperparameter tuning of $(\lambda,\eta)$, which introduces the difficulty of choosing loss functions to trade off average size and singleton probability (an issue we discussed in our first response). To fully evaluate the performance of the score the reviewer suggested, we consider three losses: $\mathbb{E}[|C(x)|+I(|C(x)|>1]$, $\mathbb{E}[0.1*|C(x)|+I(|C(x)|>1]$ and $\mathbb{E}[I(|C(x)|>1]$, and for each loss, we tune $(\lambda,\eta)$ to minimize the loss in the tuning set. 
As the losses are discontinuous and don't have clear structures (such as monotonicity), we didn't find easy ways to optimize for $(\lambda, \eta)$, therefore, we consider grid search over $(\lambda, \eta)$.
 The grid we use is $\{0.002, 0.01, 0.05, 0.25, 1.0\}$ for $\lambda$ and $\{0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0\}$ for $\eta$. Since grid search over $(\lambda,\eta)$ is computationally expensive and quite slow, we only average the results over 20 random splits. Here are the results:

 Finally, we thank the reviewer for pointing us to [9]. We already compared against the CPL framework empirically in Appendix D.3, where we treat CPL as a strong length-optimization baseline that is complementary to our singleton-oriented objective. Conceptually, we agree that “encouraging singleton prediction sets” is a natural extension of their framework, and that aligning the CPL objective with ours is an interesting research direction.

However, technically this is not a matter of simply swapping the loss. The infinite-sample theory of [9] relies crucially on the linearity of the length functional $\mathbb{E}[\text{len}(C(X))]$ in the set indicator $C(x,y)$, which allows them to recast the problem as an (infinite-dimensional) linear program and prove strong duality and conditional guarantees. Replacing length by our “singleton objective” term $I(|C(X)|>1)$ (or $I(|C(X)|>1)+\lambda |C(X)|$) produces a non-convex, discontinuous objective even after the standard $[0,1]$ relaxation of $C$, so the LP structure and strong duality arguments in [9] no longer apply. Extending CPL to handle such non-convex objectives would require reworking their duality and conditional-validity analysis from the ground up, which we view as a substantial and interesting follow-up project rather than a quick modification within the scope of this paper.

We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important point. We agree with the reviewer that when the true $p(y|x)$ is given, the simplest way to achieve conditional validity is APS [2], which includes classes from highest to lowest probability
until their sum just exceeds the threshold. However, in real machine learning tasks, we do not have access to such an oracle. APS [2] also uses split conformal prediction to achieve marginal coverage. 
To be clear, in practice, their method does not achieve conditional coverage. 
Therefore, we do not necessarily believe that achieving conditional coverage, when the true probabilities are given, is the most important goal, because, in reality, we always have to face scenarios where the conditional probabilities are not given. Thus, it is more meaningful to study criteria for this setting. 

There are some other frameworks that aim to provide conditional guarantees, even when the true probabilities are not known, such as [3]. 
To approximately achieve conditional coverage, one can also incorporate our non-conformity score into these existing frameworks. While our paper implements it using standard split conformal prediction, the score itself can be seamlessly integrated into existing frameworks that aim for conditional coverage. For example, our SOCOP score $r(x,y)$ could be directly used as the input non-conformity score $S(x,y)$ in recent work [2]. Specifically, our SOCOP score $r(x,y)$ can be plugged into their augmented quantile regression objective (their Equation (2.4)). Moreover, another research question could be if one can design a SOCOP-like nonconformity score that is directly aware and targeted for conditional coverage. This might require rethinking the foundations and derivation of SOCOP from the beginning and retracing the steps that we have taken but with a conditional aware optimization objective such as the one from [2]. This direction could potentially be challenging, but it remains interesting for future work.

## Weaknesses

> **Weakness 1**  The practical significance of the proposed objective could be further elaborated. While the goal of maximizing singletons is intuitive, the paper could benefit from a more direct discussion on the distinction between the method's singleton predictions and simply using the standard top-1 prediction. A clearer explanation of the trade-offs would help readers understand when the statistical guarantees of a conformal singleton justify the method's complexity, especially since it can still produce non-singleton sets.

We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. The key distinction between our SOCOP and the standard top-1 predictor lies in the statistical guarantee. A top-1 prediction has no statistical guarantee. Specifically, if we have a relatively inaccurate classifier, for instance, one that achieves only 70\% accuracy, then the top-one predictions will not achieve a high level of coverage/correctness, such as 95\%. Of course, one could instead output top-$k$ sets until the top-$k$ accuracy reaches 95%, possibly selecting $k$ via conformal prediction.

However, this naive approach outputs a uniformly sized and potentially large prediction set for every individual input. It is more desirable to output small prediction sets for at least some of the inputs. This motivates conformal prediction with more general nonconformity scores, such as $\hat{p}(Y|X)$. However, these classical nonconformity scores target other objectives, such as minimizing expected set size, rather than maximizing singleton predictions.

In contrast, our SOCOP score is optimized to increase the probability of producing singleton predictions while ensuring that on average the true label is contained in the prediction set with probability at least $1-\alpha$. This requires formulating and solving a new optimization problem to design a new non-conformity score and then leveraging an appropriate version of conformal prediction (split conformal prediction in our case) in order to obtain finite sample guarantees.

> **Weakness 2** The method introduces a hyperparameter, $\lambda$, that requires tuning, which can be a practical challenge. The paper could provide a more in-depth discussion on the sensitivity of the results to the choice of $\lambda$. It might also be beneficial to explore the potential impact of tuning bias on the final performance, a topic investigated in recent work such as [1], and consider if more principled selection methods could be developed.

We thank the reviewer for raising these important practical considerations. In fact, **our paper already provides a detailed analysis of $\lambda$'s role and effect**. We have provided a detailed sensitivity analysis of the effect of $\lambda$ in Section 3.1.1 and Figure 2, demonstrating that it acts as a smooth control parameter for the trade-off between average set size and non-singleton probability. The experiments demonstrate that the performance is stable to small changes in $\lambda$, but meanwhile, the model performance can be steered smoothly and reliably with larger changes in $\lambda$ as desired. Practitioners can choose $\lambda$ according to their own preference by drawing the tradeoff plot (the right panel of Figure 2) on their tuning dataset. For full analysis, we provide comprehensive tables in the Appendix showing performance across a variety of $\lambda$ values (Tables 5-9 for ImageNet-Val and Tables 11-15 for ImageNet-V2). We hope that this detailed analysis provides sufficient in-depth discussion to the behavior and role of $\lambda$. If there are any further specific questions you would like to ask, we are happy to investigate. 

Second, **our experimental design protocol explicitly avoids the "tuning bias"** the reviewer mentions. We recognize that, in general, data-dependent hyperparameter selection can introduce tuning bias in finite-sample coverage, as discussed by [1]. summary.value:
**Summary**

This paper addresses a key limitation of conformal prediction: while it creates reliable prediction sets (e.g., a list of possible answers that is 95% likely to contain the true one), these sets often contain multiple items, making them ambiguous for automated decision-making. The authors argue that the most useful outcome is a set with just one answer (a "singleton"), as it provides a clear, actionable result. 
They introduce a method called SOCOP (Singleton-Optimized Conformal Prediction) which is specifically designed to maximize the frequency of these singleton predictions. 
Instead of only trying to make the prediction sets as small as possible on average, SOCOP try to produce unambiguous, single-answer outputs, creating a more practical trade-off for real-world applications where decision clarity is more important than a slightly smaller average set size.


**Contribution**

The main contribution is a novel and highly efficient method to achieve this goal. 
The authors derive a new "nonconformity score" from an optimization objective that directly penalizes non-singleton sets. 
Their key innovation is a geometric insight that transforms the complex task of calculating this score into a simple computational geometry problem: finding the lower convex hull of a set of 2D points. 
This allows the score to be computed in fast time, making the method practical even for problems with thousands of classes. 
Experiments on image classification and large language models show that SOCOP significantly increases the rate of singleton predictions (often by over 20%) with only a minimal cost to the average set size, proving its effectiveness and practical value.

*   The paper's main strength lies in its novel objective function and the corresponding insight into evaluating conformal prediction. By shifting the focus from minimizing average set size to minimizing the probability of non-singleton sets (`P(size > 1)`), the work introduces a practical and well-motivated criterion for efficiency that directly relates to the goal of automated decision-making. This reframing provides a valuable perspective on what constitutes a "useful" prediction set in many real-world applications.

*   This conceptual contribution is supported by a thorough and well-explained computational algorithm. The paper provides a deep discussion on how to make the proposed nonconformity score practical, culminating in an efficient O(K) method based on a geometric reformulation involving the lower convex hull. This ensures the method is not just a theoretical construct but a scalable tool that can be readily applied.

*   The work can be seen as a natural and timely extension of recent research on improving the efficiency of conformal sets, such as the work on length optimization by [1]. While that paper focused on minimizing the expected set size, this paper explores a related but distinct objective—maximizing singleton frequency. This progression shows a thoughtful engagement with the state-of-the-art and pushes the conversation forward on defining and optimizing different notions of efficiency in conformal prediction.

Thank you for this insightful suggestion. You are correct that our current submission focuses on split conformal prediction that targets to achieve marginal coverage. However, our proposed SOCOP non-conformity score is designed to be modular. While our paper implements it using standard split conformal prediction, the score itself can be seamlessly integrated into existing frameworks that aim for conditional coverage.

## Questions

> **Question 1.** Can you provide more intuition in the paragraph “Computing the nonconformity score”? My attempt is “The conformal score is the smallest “price” $\eta$ in terms of the set size metric (singleton + size objective) per unit of “coverage” such that if we “buy” all classes with price less than $\eta$, we will have purchased the true class. I'm not sure if this is precisely correct, but something like this would be useful.

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question and intuition. Indeed, the proposed intuition captures the essence of our construction. Our nonconformity score $r(x,y)$ is derived from the Lagrangian objective $\ell_{\gamma,\lambda}(S;\eta) = \mathbb{I}(|S|>1) + \lambda|S|-\eta   \sum_{y \in S} \gamma_y$. To clarify this intuition, define $\operatorname{Cost}(S) = \mathbb{I}(|S|>1) + \lambda|S|$ as the cost of penalizing non-singleton sets, and $\operatorname{Benefit}(S) = \sum_{y \in S} \gamma_y$ as the benefit of covered probability mass. The multiplier $\eta\geq0$ can indeed be viewed as the price per unit of benefit (coverage). 

For each fixed $\eta$, the optimal set $S_{\eta, \gamma} \in \arg\min_{S \subseteq \mathcal{Y}} \ell_{\gamma,\lambda}(S;\eta)$ minimizes the net cost given this "price" $\eta$. As $\eta$ increases, the optimization is incentivized to "purchase" more coverage, leading to nested sets $S_{\eta_1, \gamma} \subseteq S_{\eta_2, \gamma}$ for $\eta_1<\eta_2$ (Lemma B.1). Our score, $r(x,y) := \inf\\{\eta \ge 0 : y \in S_{\eta,\gamma}\\}$, thus quantifies the entry price at which the true label $y$ is first included in the optimal set. 

To summarize, your interpretation is correct: the score $r(x, y_{true})$ is the minimum "price" $\eta$ required to "purchase" the true class. We will add this clarifying intuition to our revised version.

> **Question 2.** Why do you use Plug-In sets (which do not have a marginal coverage guarantee) instead of APS (which is essentially the same procedure but with the threshold tuned to achieve a marginal coverage guarantee)?

Thank you for this point. The term Plug-In sets in our paper follows the definition of the naive prediction sets from [1], which includes classes from highest to lowest probability until their sum just exceeds the threshold $1-\alpha$. This method serves as a non-conformal baseline.

You are correct that APS is the same procedure but with conformal calibration. We did not include APS as a separate baseline because RAPS is a stronger version of APS for set-size efficiency. Moreover, APS is a special case of RAPS with $\lambda=0$, and in our experiments with ImageNet, we observed that $\lambda=0$ was never selected, confirming that RAPS outperforms APS. So we omitted APS, but we are happy to include it as a separate baseline if you prefer. (Though we would appreciate a justification of why to do this.)

[1] Anastasios Nikolas Angelopoulos, Stephen Bates, Michael Jordan, and Jitendra Malik. Uncertainty sets for image classifiers using conformal prediction. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2021. URL https://openreview.net/forum?id=eNdiU_DbM9.

> **Question 4**  For theorem part, is there any insight for the $P(size <1)$'s increasing under proposed method?

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. In the classification task,  $\text{size}<1$ corresponds to empty sets. When $\lambda=0$ (pure singleton limit, see Section 2.2, Corollary 2.5), the resulting split conformal prediction sets are either the top-1 label $\left\\{y_1\right\\}$ if $\hat{p}\left(y_1 \mid x\right) \geqslant c$, for some quantity $c$, or the whole set $\mathcal{Y}$ otherwise. Hence, the procedure will never produce empty sets. However, we agree that when $\lambda>0$, the method can produce empty sets. In our construction, the prediction set at a test point $x$ is $\widehat{C}(x)=\left\\{y: r_\lambda(x, y) \leq \hat{q}\right\\}$, where $\hat{q}$ is the calibrated threshold. Because the scores are non-decreasing, i.e., $r_\lambda(x, y_1)\leq r_\lambda(x, y_2)\leq...\leq r_\lambda(x, y_K)$, $\widehat{C}(x)=\varnothing$ is equivalent to $r_\lambda(x, y_1)>\hat{q}$. One can show that $r_\lambda\left(x, y_1\right)=\frac{\lambda}{\hat{p}\left(y_1 \mid x\right)}$, hence $\widehat{C}(x)=\varnothing$ if and only if $\hat{p}\left(y_1 \mid x\right)<\frac{\lambda}{\hat{q}}$. When the model is very uncertain about an input x, the probability of its top prediction, $\hat{p}(y_1|x)$, can be lower than $\frac{\lambda}{\hat{q}}$, resulting an empty set. In such cases, SOCOP produces an empty set, which can be viewed as the model appropriately abstaining from prediction due to low confidence.

Empirically, the rate of empty sets for SOCOP was negligible ($<0.01\%$) across all experiments, which was comparable to other baseline methods. As this metric did not reveal a meaningful difference, we omitted it from our result tables for conciseness. This confirms that while the theoretical possibility exists, it does not negatively impact the utility of the method in standard classification tasks.
